## Description

The Python 3 program reads an integer sequence from standard input and prints the sum of the minimum numbers of erase operations needed to clear each nonempty contiguous subarray. An operation may erase a consecutive interval of integer values only if every value in that interval is currently present. It erases every occurrence of those values.

## Preconditions

- **PRE-1 (Unverified)** — The first input line contains an integer \(N\) with \(1 \le N \le 300{,}000\).
- **PRE-2 (Unverified)** — The second input line contains exactly \(N\) integers in sequence order, each between \(1\) and \(N\) inclusive.

## Postconditions

- **POST-1 (Unverified)** — Every pair of positions \(1 \le L \le R \le N\) contributes exactly once, even when different pairs select identical values.
- **POST-2 (Unverified)** — Each pair contributes the minimum number of legal operations needed to erase its subarray. This equals the number of maximal consecutive runs among the distinct values in that subarray. Within a fixed subarray, the order and multiplicity of those values do not affect its contribution.
- **POST-3 (Unverified)** — Standard output contains a single integer equal to the exact sum of all contributions. A singleton subarray contributes \(1\), so an input with \(N=1\) produces \(1\).

## Test suggestions

- Use \(N=1\) and sequence `1`. Expect `1`. (PRE-1, PRE-2, POST-1, POST-3)
- Use `1 3 1` with \(N=3\). Expect `9`. The full subarray contributes \(2\) because value `2` is missing, and both copies of `1` can be erased together. (POST-1, POST-2, POST-3)
- Use `3 1 2` with \(N=3\). Expect `7`. The full subarray contributes \(1\) because its values form a consecutive interval. (POST-2, POST-3)
- Use \(N=300{,}000\) with every entry equal to `1`. Expect `45000150000`. (PRE-1, POST-1, POST-3)

## Unspecified behavior

Behavior for input outside PRE-1 or PRE-2 is unspecified. The choice among equally short sequences of erase operations is unspecified.
